name: Rio de Janeiro
tagline: Samba, surf and granite peaks where the rainforest meets the sea
description:
Few cities have a setting as outrageous as Rio's. Forest-cloaked granite peaks plunge straight into the Atlantic, Christ the Redeemer spreads his arms over it all, and long crescents of golden sand are lined with volleyball nets, coconut stands and some of the world's most confident sunbathers. Cariocas, as locals are called, treat the beach as a shared living room, and joining them to applaud the sunset from Arpoador rock is practically a civic duty.

Beyond the postcard views, Rio runs on rhythm. Samba spills out of the bars of Lapa and the old port district where Afro-Brazilian culture took root, while the hilltop lanes of Santa Teresa hide artists' studios and faded colonial mansions. A football match at the Maracanã is a near-religious experience, and the Tijuca rainforest offers waterfall hikes only minutes from downtown.

Food is generous and unfussy: skewers of picanha at a churrascaria, crisp pastéis and sugarcane juice at a street market, ice-cold chopp at a corner boteco. Carnival turns the whole city into a five-day party, but Rio rewards visitors year-round. Just travel smart, keep valuables out of sight and follow local advice about where to go after dark.

safety.notes: Street crime is a real concern: carry only what you need, keep your phone out of sight on the street and the beach, and use Uber or 99 rather than walking after dark. Never enter a favela without a reputable local guide, and don't resist if you are robbed.

tipping: Restaurants usually add a 10% service charge ('serviço') that covers the tip, so extra is optional; beach vendors and taxi drivers don't expect tips, though rounding up is appreciated.
gettingAround: The clean, air-conditioned Metro links Centro, Botafogo, Copacabana, Ipanema and Barra, and Uber or 99 rides are cheap and the safest option at night. By day, walking or cycling the beachfront promenades is a joy.
tips: Take only a sarong, some cash and a cheap phone to the beach; locals leave passports, jewelry and cameras at home.
Book the first cog train up to Christ the Redeemer and check the summit webcam before you go, since clouds can swallow the statue entirely.
Beach barracas rent chairs and umbrellas and run a tab for drinks; pay when you leave, and remember your lifeguard post number to find your spot again.
On Sundays and holidays, the beachfront road along Copacabana, Ipanema and Leblon closes to cars and fills with cyclists, skaters and families.
Ride the Sugarloaf cable cars about 90 minutes before sunset to see the city in daylight, at golden hour and lit up at night.
Ipanema's Sunday Hippie Fair in Praça General Osório is the best place for local crafts, leather sandals and street-food snacks.
etiquette: Friends greet with a kiss on each cheek; a handshake is fine when meeting someone for the first time.
Avoid the 'OK' hand sign, which is rude in Brazil; a thumbs-up is the all-purpose gesture of approval.
Swimwear is for the beach, so throw on a shirt and shorts before heading into shops, restaurants or the Metro.
Social plans run on relaxed time and arriving 20–30 minutes late is normal, but be punctual for tours and reservations.

neighborhoods.name: Ipanema
neighborhoods.blurb: Leafy streets of boutiques, juice bars and restaurants behind Rio's chicest beach, where applauding the sunset from Arpoador is a nightly ritual.

neighborhoods.name: Copacabana
neighborhoods.blurb: A dense, lively strip of high-rises and kiosks along the famous crescent beach, with good-value hotels and round-the-clock energy.

neighborhoods.name: Santa Teresa
neighborhoods.blurb: A bohemian hilltop quarter of crumbling mansions, artists' studios and quiet bars, reached by the rattling yellow tram.

neighborhoods.name: Lapa
neighborhoods.blurb: Rio's samba heartland, where historic dance halls and street parties roar beneath the white arches until dawn on weekends.

neighborhoods.name: Botafogo
neighborhoods.blurb: A buzzing bayside district of craft-beer bars, creative restaurants and hostels, with knockout views of Sugarloaf across the water.

dishes.name: Feijoada
dishes.description: A slow-cooked stew of black beans and assorted pork, traditionally eaten on Saturdays with rice, farofa, sautéed collard greens and orange slices.

dishes.name: Picanha
dishes.description: The prized top-sirloin cap, salted with coarse salt, grilled on skewers and carved tableside at churrascarias.

dishes.name: Pastel
dishes.description: A crisp, bubbly fried pastry stuffed with cheese, ground beef or shrimp, best eaten hot at a street market with a glass of sugarcane juice.

dishes.name: Açaí na tigela
dishes.description: Frozen açaí pulp blended thick and topped with banana and granola; in Rio it's a post-beach energy fix rather than a health trend.

dishes.name: Caipirinha
dishes.description: Brazil's national cocktail of muddled lime, sugar and cachaça over crushed ice; ask for it with passion fruit or other tropical fruits.

events.name: Rio Carnival
events.description: Samba schools parade through the Sambadrome with thousands of costumed dancers and towering floats, while hundreds of free street parties called blocos take over every neighborhood.

events.name: Festa Junina
events.description: June festivals celebrate rural traditions with square dancing, bonfires, checked shirts, mulled wine called quentão and corn-based sweets.

events.name: Festival do Rio
events.description: The city's international film festival screens hundreds of Brazilian and world films in cinemas across town over two busy weeks.

events.name: Réveillon
events.description: Around two million people dressed in white pack Copacabana for New Year's Eve concerts and a spectacular fireworks show over the sea, tossing flowers to the sea goddess Iemanjá.

attractions.name: Christ the Redeemer
attractions.description: The 30-meter Art Deco statue stands atop Corcovado mountain with arms flung wide, and the panorama from its base takes in beaches, lagoon, Sugarloaf and ocean in one sweep. The cog railway rattling up through the rainforest is half the fun.
attractions.bookingTip: Book the first cog train of the day online and check the summit webcam first, because clouds can hide the statue completely.

attractions.name: Sugarloaf Mountain
attractions.description: Two glass cable cars swing you from Praia Vermelha up to the summit of this rounded granite peak guarding the mouth of Guanabara Bay. Go in the late afternoon to watch the sun sink behind Christ the Redeemer as the city lights flicker on below.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy tickets online and ride up about 90 minutes before sunset to beat the evening queue at the Urca station.

attractions.name: Copacabana Beach
attractions.description: Four kilometers of golden sand edged by the famous black-and-white wave mosaic promenade, lined with kiosks serving ice-cold coconuts and caipirinhas. Mornings bring footvolley games and joggers; evenings bring beach bars, live samba and a glittering line of hotel lights.
attractions.bookingTip: Rent a chair and umbrella from a beach barraca and settle up when you leave, keeping only a little cash and a cheap phone on you.

attractions.name: Ipanema Beach
attractions.description: Rio's most stylish stretch of sand, where each lifeguard post draws its own tribe, from surfers and families to the LGBTQ+ crowd near Posto 8. Stay for sunset, when the crowd on Arpoador rock applauds as the sun slides behind the Dois Irmãos peaks.
attractions.bookingTip: Claim a spot on Arpoador rock 45 minutes before sunset and keep a firm grip on your phone in the crowd.

attractions.name: Selarón Steps
attractions.description: Chilean artist Jorge Selarón spent more than two decades covering these 215 steps with over 2,000 tiles from more than 60 countries, many sent by admirers. The result is a riot of red, green and yellow linking the nightlife of Lapa with hilltop Santa Teresa.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive before 9 a.m. for crowd-free photos, and climb with a group or guide rather than alone.

attractions.name: Tijuca Forest
attractions.description: A hand-replanted Atlantic rainforest sprawling over the mountains in the middle of the city, where capuchin monkeys, toucans and waterfalls hide along well-marked trails. Hike to Pico da Tijuca for a summit panorama or take the easy stroll to the Cascatinha Taunay falls.
attractions.bookingTip: Hike with a licensed guide or on busy weekend mornings, and start early to beat the heat and afternoon storms.

attractions.name: Museum of Tomorrow
attractions.description: Santiago Calatrava's skeletal white building juts out over Guanabara Bay like a spacecraft, anchoring the revitalized port district. Inside, immersive bilingual exhibits on climate, population and the future of life on Earth are genuinely thought-provoking.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy timed tickets online, and skip Tuesdays when free entry brings long lines.

attractions.name: Maracanã Stadium
attractions.description: Brazil's temple of football has hosted two World Cup finals, and a Flamengo or Fluminense match here is a thunderous spectacle of drums, flags and chanting. On non-match days, stadium tours visit the dressing rooms and walk you out through the players' tunnel.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy match tickets through the clubs' official sites or a reputable tour with transport, and never wear the rival team's colors.

attractions.name: Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden
attractions.description: Founded by the Portuguese prince regent in 1808, the garden's avenue of towering imperial palms is one of Rio's most elegant sights. Wander past orchid houses and ponds of giant Amazonian water lilies while marmosets scamper through the branches overhead.
attractions.bookingTip: Come right at opening on a weekday for cool air, active wildlife and empty palm avenues for photos.

attractions.name: Lapa Arches
attractions.description: Built in the 1700s to carry fresh water from the hills, the aqueduct's 42 white arches now carry the yellow Santa Teresa tram and frame Rio's most famous party district. After dark, samba bars, street vendors and open-air crowds spill out beneath them.
attractions.bookingTip: Ride the tram across the arches by day, then come back on a Friday night for the street party carrying only the cash you need.

hotels.name: Palacete Dois Irmãos
hotels.description: A sleek oceanfront tower with a rooftop infinity pool aimed squarely at the Dois Irmãos peaks, rooms paneled in reclaimed Brazilian hardwood and a spa using Amazonian botanicals. Beach butlers set up your chairs, umbrella and chilled coconut on the sand across the street.

hotels.name: Casarão das Buganvílias
hotels.description: A restored 1890s mansion clinging to the Santa Teresa hillside, with shuttered high-ceilinged rooms, a mosaic-tiled plunge pool and hammocks strung above the bay. The yellow tram rattles past the gate on its way down to Lapa.

hotels.name: Hostel Chinelo Botafogo
hotels.description: A friendly hostel in a pastel townhouse near Botafogo's Metro, with air-conditioned dorms, a caipirinha bar in the back garden and group outings to the beach and samba nights. The Sugarloaf cable car is a short bus ride away.

hotels.name: Hotel Ondulação
hotels.description: Inspired by the wave-patterned promenade outside, this design hotel curves everything, from headboards and balconies to the rooftop pool, in black and white stone. Sea-view rooms have floor-to-ceiling glass and hanging wicker chairs.

hotels.name: Palmeiras Garden Flats
hotels.description: Leafy one- and two-bedroom flats on a quiet street below Corcovado, each with a kitchen and a balcony facing the forest. The Botanical Garden, the lagoon jogging loop and Leblon's restaurants are all a short walk away.

hotels.name: Hotel Armazém do Cais
hotels.description: A 1910s coffee warehouse on the revitalized waterfront, restored with iron columns, brick vaults and rooms named after samba pioneers from the surrounding Little Africa district. The terrace looks across to the Museum of Tomorrow and the bay.

restaurants.name: Pastelaria Ventania
restaurants.description: A tiled corner counter frying crackling, rectangular pastéis to order, stuffed with cheese, ground beef or shrimp with creamy catupiry. Wash one down with fresh-pressed sugarcane juice and lime, especially before a match when the queue is half the fun.
restaurants.signatureDish: Shrimp and catupiry pastel with caldo de cana

restaurants.name: Maracujá Azul Sucos
restaurants.description: A classic Carioca juice bar with a wall of tropical fruit, from cajá and acerola to graviola and cupuaçu, blended to order alongside thick açaí bowls for post-beach refueling. Stand at the counter with the surfers and add a toasted ham-and-cheese on the side.
restaurants.signatureDish: Açaí bowl with banana and granola

restaurants.name: Café Bondinho Amarelo
restaurants.description: A sunny hilltop café where pão de queijo comes out of the oven every 20 minutes and single-origin coffee from Minas Gerais is brewed by the cup. Grab a window stool to watch the tram clatter past.
restaurants.signatureDish: Warm pão de queijo with Minas Gerais coffee

restaurants.name: Mata & Mar
restaurants.description: Set in a glass pavilion wrapped in ferns, this tasting menu roams from Amazonian river fish to Atlantic seafood and Minas cheeses, using native ingredients like tucupi, jambu and baru nuts. The sommelier pours wines from Brazil's southern highlands alongside aged cachaças.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pirarucu with tucupi broth and jambu

restaurants.name: Churrascaria Laço Gaúcho
restaurants.description: Waiters in gaucho dress circle the room with sizzling skewers of picanha, lamb, sausage and garlic beef until you flip your table card to red. The buffet of hearts of palm, feijoada and quail eggs could be a meal on its own.

restaurants.name: Botequim Tamborim Rachado
restaurants.description: Plastic tables spill onto the sidewalk, chopp arrives in small glasses so it never gets warm, and a samba circle strikes up around a back table by 10 p.m. Order salt-cod fritters and shrimp pastéis by the plateful.

restaurants.name: Tacho da Gamboa
restaurants.description: A family-run kitchen in Rio's historic Little Africa, famous for its Saturday feijoada served to the sound of a live samba circle in the courtyard. Weekday lunches bring moqueca, okra stews and generous set plates.
restaurants.signatureDish: Feijoada completa with farofa and collard greens

restaurants.name: Hanami na Baía
restaurants.description: A pocket-sized sushi counter on the Urca seawall, where the chef marries Japanese technique with Brazilian fruit and fish, such as tuna with cashew fruit and sea bass with passion-fruit ponzu. Arrive for sunset, when the bay glows behind Christ the Redeemer.
restaurants.signatureDish: Sea bass sashimi with passion-fruit ponzu

experiences.name: Samba School Rehearsal Night
experiences.description: Join thousands of dancers, drummers and fans at a samba school's pre-Carnival rehearsal, a thunderous, sweat-soaked party held from spring through February. Your guide teaches the basic steps on the way and handles tickets and safe transport.

experiences.name: Tandem Hang Glide from Pedra Bonita
experiences.description: Run off a wooden ramp more than 500 meters above São Conrado and soar over rainforest and ocean with a certified pilot before landing on the beach below. Flights depend on the wind, so keep your morning flexible.

experiences.name: Guanabara Bay Sunset Schooner
experiences.description: Sail a wooden schooner around the base of Sugarloaf and past the old forts of Guanabara Bay as the sun drops behind the mountains. A bossa nova duo plays on deck while the bar keeps the caipirinhas coming.

experiences.name: Santa Teresa Art & Flavors Walk
experiences.description: Climb from the Selarón Steps into Santa Teresa's cobbled lanes with a local artist, stopping at open studios, a cachaça bar and family-run kitchens. Tastings include pastéis, acarajé, brigadeiros and a bowl of hearty bean broth.
